# Samples

Each directory here holds frames of the game that a test feeds to the core and checks the reading of. Every file in one must read as its name (or its readings file) says, or as unreadable, never as something else. A frame the core ever read wrong becomes a sample here: a Bug Report's `crops/` has it already, cut and named as the directory's rule says. Names may only come from the maintainer's own Characters, or from players who agree to it in the Bug Report flow; any other player's name or chat is cut or painted out before a frame is committed.

To check many new frames at once, tile them into contact sheets, each frame labelled with its file name: `python scripts/contact-sheet.py <folder-or-png>... [--out <folder>] [--tile <px>]` writes them to `_scratch/contact/` (it needs Pillow). Look over every sheet for a name or chat these rules don't allow. A whole client area shrunk to a tile can hide a name, so give those a larger `--tile`.

## `minimap`

Every file in `samples/minimap` must be recognised against the map names fixture, `crates/minerva-core/tests/fixtures/osms-map-names.json`; there, a `--window` sample's client area is fed whole, and the title is found in it wherever it is (ADR 0021). Each is also fed scaled to other UI Sizes, where it must read as its map or as unreadable, never as another (`tests/minimap_samples.rs`). A title ever read wrong becomes a sample there: a Bug Report's `crops/minimap-title-<ms>.png` is one already. A title ever not found becomes a `--window` sample: a Bug Report's `crops/title-capture-<ms>.png`, kept whole where no title was found for 10 s, is one already, renamed to that shape, with any other player's name or chat in it painted out.

## `exp-bar`

Every file in `samples/exp-bar` must read as its name (or its recording's `readings.json`) says, or as unreadable, never as a wrong number, in two layers (ADR 0017): the files there are the EXP figures alone, fed as a frame of them (`tests/exp_bar_samples.rs`), and the `--window` samples in `samples/minimap` are found in their Status Bar and read too. A number ever read wrong becomes a sample of the figures there: a Bug Report's `crops/exp-bar-<ms>.png` is one already. A Status Bar whose figures are ever not found, or found in the wrong place, becomes a sample of the bottom of the client area, its name's line painted over as for `samples/status-bar` unless that rule allows it: `samples/exp-bar/<exp>__<percent>--<what>-strip.png`, the client area's full width, fed whole as a Status Bar capture, with no other player's name or chat in it. A Bug Report's `crops/status-bar-strip-<ms>.png`, the strip kept whole where no Status Bar was found, is such a sample already, renamed to that shape: its name's line painted over unless that rule allows it, and any chat in it painted out.

## `item-tooltip`

Every file in `samples/item-tooltip` must read as the item its name says (or as no Item Tooltip, for `no-tooltip`), or as unreadable, never as another item (`tests/item_tooltip_samples.rs`). A frame that is ever read wrong becomes a sample there: a Bug Report's `crops/item-tooltip-<ms>@<x>,<y>.png` is one already, renamed `<item-name>@<x>,<y>.png`, cropped to the tooltip so no other player's name or chat is committed (the pointer's spot moved with it).

## `player-shop`

Every file in `samples/player-shop` must read as its readings say (`<name>.json`: each listing not sold out, with its item's name, quantity and mesos, or `{ "covered": true }` for one the pointer or the game's tooltip covers), or as unreadable ("?"), never as another item or price (`tests/player_shop_samples.rs`). A frame that is ever read wrong becomes a sample there: a Bug Report's `crops/player-shop-<ms>.png` is one already, cropped to the shop's list so no seller's name or chat is committed. Where no shop was found, a Bug Report keeps the whole client area instead, `crops/client-area-<ms>.png`: a frame to cut to the shop's list in the same way, with the margin `crops/player-shop-<ms>.png` keeps, before it is committed. A scroll's listing whose name the game cut short also says its `"tier"` (`"Lesser"`, `"Intermediate"`, `"Greater"` or `"Chaos"`), as its picture shows it, and only such a listing does: the test's made-up world gives it four scrolls of that start, one of each tier, so only the picture names it. A listing whose name the game cut short so that it could be several items also says `"named"`: the item its Item Tooltip names, "?" until hovered unless it is a scroll its picture names. `<name>@<x>,<y>.png` is `<name>.png`'s shop with the pointer at (x, y) on a listing and the tooltip by it, fed after `<name>.png`: cut as the list is but as far right as the tooltip's name line, the rest of the chat painted out, and the chat showing through the tooltip painted its fill.

## `status-bar`

Every file in `samples/status-bar` must read as its name says (`<level>__<job>__<Name>--<what>.png`; `<level>__<job>--<what>.png` for a crop with the name taken out; `no-status-bar--<what>.png`), or as unreadable, never as another level, job or name (`tests/status_bar_samples.rs`). A frame that is ever read wrong becomes a sample there: a Bug Report's `crops/status-bar-<ms>.png` is one already, cut to the level, job and name. Names may only come from the maintainer's own Characters, or from players who agree to it in the Bug Report flow; any other crop is cut down to the level and job before it is committed, its name's line painted over in the bar's plain slate (58,67,72).

## `pickup-log`

Each directory is a short sequence of 10 Hz log-band crops, named by capture milliseconds,
with `truth.json` listing the arrivals checked by eye, oldest first. Its first frame is a
baseline: lines already there are not arrivals. `source` identifies the maintainer's
2026-10-25 party (`1025`) or 2026-10-07 solo (`1007`) recording. Frames are cut to a 325×139
band at client (1590,830) in both recordings, checked against the source frames. The
2026-10-25 recording was captured at client (1400,730), 520×260: the committed clips
start at (190,100) within it. The 2026-10-07 recording was captured at client
(1560,780), 355×220: the clips start at (30,50) within it. The closing parentheses and six
22 px slots are kept, and the lines end 6 px inside the clip's right edge (11 to 12 px in the game's); the reader is given the UI Size only, never a log position.
Each clip must count only its arrivals, never more. An unlocated empty baseline cannot
prove the log is empty: the first located stack establishes the baseline, so those first
lines may be missed. At other UI Sizes it may read fewer, never another line (`tests/pickup_log_samples.rs`). The `covered` clip has another player's
entire name plate painted black in frames 6600–7200, including its border. All other clips
contain no player names. A Bug Report's `crops/pickup-log-<ms>.png` belongs in a short
sequence showing the frame before and after the problem, with the same privacy rule.

## `pickup-log-band`

Whole 400×480 captures of the Pickup Log's band, as `PanelState::pickup_log_capture` asks for it
at the samples' UI Size on a 1920×1200 client area, from the Bug Report of 0.15.0 at 2026-10-26
07:02 (Perion, Deep Valley and Perion Dungeon Entrance: rock, brick and cloud backgrounds, with
the game's quickslots and Cash Shop button in the band's bottom-left) and the one at 09:03
(Ellinia: bright greens and a white sky, over which the lines were read wrong). Named
`<kind>--<capture ms>.png`: `log--` shows lines of the Pickup Log (fading, covered by Mobs, or
fresh), `no-log--` shows none, and `lines--` are the six frames, in order, of the 09:03 report
whose lines are plainly legible: mesos (+13) and `Squishy Liquid x1 earned. (Etc)` arrive in
183631, another `Squishy Liquid x1` in 187992 and `Slime Bubble x1 earned. (Etc)` in 188167
(an EXP (+2) line arrived unseen between 184483 and 187992, in a crop the report left out).
A `lines--` clip reads as those lines, whole, in order (`tests/pickup_log_samples.rs`).
Lines end at band x≈390 and the newest is at band y≈240. A `log--` frame is never found anywhere
else, and a `no-log--` one finds none (`tests/pickup_log_samples.rs`). The only name in them is the
maintainer's own Character's, `Egbert`; a fragment of another name above it in `log--238612` is
painted over.

## `pickup-log-720p`

Short sequences of 10 Hz crops of the Pickup Log at a UI Size of about 0.64 of the samples' (a
Status Bar 35 px high against 55: a 1280×720 client area), from the maintainer's own 2026-10-26
recording on The Murky Swamp II, where the Bug Report of 0.15.0 at 14:41 never found the log. Lines
are 14 px apart and the text 10 px tall, drawn by the game at that size, not scaled from the other
samples. Each directory is a clip, its frames named by capture milliseconds in the recording, with a
`truth.json` as in `pickup-log`: `baseline` is the first frame, whose lines are not arrivals, and
`arrivals` are the lines that came in each later frame, oldest first, checked by eye. `source` is
`720p`. A recorded crop was 320×250 at client (960,380); these are cut to 208×96 at its (112,100),
which is client (1072,480): the six line slots and their closing parentheses, the lines ending 7 px
inside the right edge, which is the client area's (as at the samples' size, 11 to 12 px). The clips
are fed as the real band is (`tests/pickup_log_720p.rs`): the band `capture_band` makes at a UI Size of
35/55 from a 1280×720 client area, 255×306 at client (1025,414), black, with the clip pasted in at
(47,66) in it, and a cold reader read at 0.636 for each clip. Each clip must count only the lines
that arrived, no earlier than the frame that brought them and no later than half a second after it (a
line is read again at the captures after it arrives, and counted when the reads vote), and tally no more mesos or Items than
arrived. At this size it may read fewer, and `Unreadable` stands for a line seen but not read:
`exp-and-mesos` (EXP, mesos, an Etc Item), `etc-and-use-items` (mesos, Etc and Use Items, a name cut
short, and a Mob's sprite over the top row for the clip's last second), `skill-effect` (a skill's
beam over the log's right end for 8 seconds, and four EXP lines arriving at once under it) and
`burst` (four EXP lines at once, two more one at a time, then a Use Item and mesos together, an Etc
Item and mesos a frame apart, over a thick, moving grass). No
clip shows a player's name: its only text besides the log is the world's. Mobs may show their own
names (the `Ligator` at the left of `etc-and-use-items`).

# mpl-ocr

A low-latency, embeddable OCR framework that reads on-screen game state from
**MapleStory Classic World**: map name, HP/MP/EXP, damage numbers, inventory,
tooltips, chat, and more. Screen pixels in, structured readings out.

> **Unofficial.** Not affiliated with or endorsed by Nexon. Screen capture
> only: no memory reading, injection, or packet inspection. You are
> responsible for complying with the game's Terms of Service. See
> [DISCLAIMER.md](DISCLAIMER.md).

**Status: prototype.** Readable today: map name, level, job, character name,
HP, MP, EXP, NPC dialogue, item and skill tooltips (beta: names mostly right, stat
lines about 60% exact so far), the item inventory
window (item icons, optionally named by you), quest helper (beta), chat (beta),
damage numbers (beta: 18 of 20 held-out numbers right, needs teaching), and an opt-in whole-screen text scan.
Other movable windows (equipment, stats, skills) reuse the same window
detector and are next. Use it from Rust, or from any language or web UI via
the local server (`mapleocr serve`, see [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md)).
Catalogue and measurements: [docs/design.md](docs/design.md).

## Build

Requires Rust (stable, MSVC toolchain) on Windows 10 2004+ / Windows 11.

```sh
cargo install --path crates/mapleocr-cli --locked   # puts `mapleocr` in ~/.cargo/bin (on PATH)
```

Open a new terminal afterwards if Rust was installed in this session. Rerun
the command after pulling changes. Without installing, use
`.\target\release\mapleocr.exe` after `cargo build --release`.

## Try it

```sh
# 1. Find the game window and save it as the default target
mapleocr targets
mapleocr select --index 0            # or: --title MapleStory / --process MapleStory.exe

# 2. Read the map name live (calibrates on first run)
mapleocr calibrate
mapleocr watch map_name
mapleocr read map_name               # one JSON reading

# Optional: teach it your maps so readings snap to exact names
mapleocr pack add-map "Victoria Road" "Henesys"

# Teach the status-bar digit sprites (once; again when new digits appear).
# Type exactly what the ROI shows; the frame is grabbed from the game.
mapleocr atlas learn --roi hp --text "[356/598]"
mapleocr atlas learn --roi exp --text "10,105[91.53%]"
mapleocr atlas learn --roi level --text "17"

# Teach the NPC dialogue window's anchor from a saved frame where it is open
mapleocr calibrate --learn-anchor npc_dialogue --image fixtures/local/<session>/0010_full.png

# Everything at once, or the whole screen as text lines
mapleocr watch
mapleocr watch screen

# Movable windows and detectors: teach the inventory title once, then name icons
mapleocr window learn item_inventory_title --image <frame.png> --rect title=815,186,320,26
mapleocr window name-icon item_inventory --image <frame.png> --slot 3=Leaf
mapleocr watch tooltip item_inventory

# 3. Record samples: press F9 in game to save a frame, Ctrl+C to stop
mapleocr capture-dataset --label "inventory open"

# 4. Measure capture cost while the game is running
mapleocr bench capture --seconds 10
```

`capture-dataset` writes PNG + JSON sidecars to `fixtures/local/` (git-ignored).
Those images contain game pixels; keep them local.

Identify the UI font from labeled crops (Python tooling in `tools/`):

```sh
python -m venv tools/.venv && tools/.venv/Scripts/pip install -e "tools[dev]"
tools/.venv/Scripts/python -m mapleocr_tools.identify_font fixtures/local/font-samples.json
```

## Use it from any language or a web UI

```sh
mapleocr serve                  # http://127.0.0.1:8765 : dashboard, REST, WebSocket
```

- `GET /v1/readings`, `GET /v1/read/hp`, `GET /v1/status`
- `ws://127.0.0.1:8765/v1/stream`: live JSON events with subscribe/unsubscribe

Examples: [Python](examples/python/client.py) and
[TypeScript](examples/web/client.ts). The server is loopback-only and rejects
browser origins you have not allowed (`--allow-origin`). Full spec:
[docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md).

## Use it from Rust

```rust
use mapleocr_core::{MapleOcr, Value};

let ocr = MapleOcr::auto()?;            // find the game window, calibrate
ocr.subscribe(&["map_name"], |r| {
    if let Value::Map(m) = &r.value { println!("{} / {}", m.region, m.name) }
})?;
```

See [crates/mapleocr-core/examples/map_name.rs](crates/mapleocr-core/examples/map_name.rs).

# Why mpl-ocr?

mpl-ocr turns MapleStory Classic World's screen into structured data: HP, MP,
EXP, item tooltips, inventory, chat, NPC dialogue, damage numbers and more. It
works from screen pixels only (no memory reading, injection, or packet
inspection) and any language or web UI can consume it over a local WebSocket.

> Unofficial, not affiliated with Nexon. You are responsible for following the
> game's Terms of Service. See [DISCLAIMER.md](../DISCLAIMER.md).

## Speed: mpl-ocr vs. general-purpose Python OCR

Same saved frames, same machine (Ryzen 5 3600, CPU only), best case for the
Python engines (they get the exact HP crop, padded and upscaled 2x).

**Reading the HP number** (12 frames, median time per read):

| engine | time | correct |
|---|---|---|
| **mpl-ocr** | **0.25 ms** | **12 / 12** |
| EasyOCR (CPU) | 125 ms (**500x slower**) | 12 / 12 |
| Tesseract | 138 ms (**550x slower**) | 11 / 12 |
| RapidOCR (PaddleOCR on ONNX) | 284 ms (**1100x slower**) | 12 / 12 |

**Reading the MP number** (the digits are smaller, and the engines struggle):

| engine | correct |
|---|---|
| **mpl-ocr** | **12 / 12** |
| EasyOCR | 10 / 12 |
| RapidOCR | 8 / 12 |
| Tesseract | 3 / 12 |

**Item tooltips from a full frame** (3 frames, 5 item names; mpl-ocr finds each
tooltip by its title bullet, the Python engines read the whole screen):

| engine | time | names found |
|---|---|---|
| **mpl-ocr** | **~60-100 ms** (first read; cached while the tooltip stays up) | 4 / 5 |
| Tesseract | 1.1 s (11-17x slower) | 5 / 5 |
| RapidOCR | 2.3 s (23-38x slower) | 4 / 5 |
| EasyOCR (CPU) | 12.6 s (**125-200x slower**) | 5 / 5 |

Tooltip accuracy is **not yet where it needs to be**: against hand-labeled lines,
mpl-ocr gets 5 of 6 names and 15 of 25 text lines exactly right (the Python engines
were scored only on whether the name appears anywhere, a more lenient test).
The speed is real; the accuracy work is in progress (see
[docs/design.md](design.md)).

**Finding the HP number anywhere on a 1920x1200 frame** (5 frames): RapidOCR
3.7 s (5/5), Tesseract 1.1 s (0/5), EasyOCR 12.7 s (0/5). mpl-ocr does not
search: it calibrates once and reads the known region in 0.25 ms.

**Why it is this much faster:** it does not run a general text model. Fixed-font
UI text and sprite digits are matched against exact glyph shapes taught from
your own screen; unchanged regions are skipped by hash, so a still screen costs
almost nothing. Measured at ~56 fps on the same machine:

| what is running | CPU |
|---|---|
| status bar + map readers (HP, MP, EXP, level, job, name, map) | **~6% of one core** |
| everything: plus chat, quest helper, tooltip / inventory / damage scouting | ~19% of one core |

A Python OCR call on the HP crop alone takes 125-284 ms, so it cannot keep up
with a single region at 60 fps, let alone all of them.

## What you can build with it

Stable = accuracy checked on held-out frames. Beta = works, with known gaps.

| capability | status | typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **HP / MP** as numbers (`current`, `max`) | stable | overlays, stream widgets, health-based alerts |
| **EXP** value and percent | stable | EXP/hour trackers, leveling analytics |
| **Level, job, character name** | stable | multi-character dashboards |
| **Map name** (snaps to your own map list) | stable | OBS scene switching, per-map stats, location logs |
| **Item tooltips** (item name + stat lines, finds the box anywhere) | **beta**: 5/6 names, ~60% of lines exact | price-lookup overlays, item databases, loot logs |
| **Inventory window** (finds it wherever you drag it; item icons recognized once you name them) | stable for detection, you name the icons | inventory trackers, drop logs, meso/item history |
| **NPC dialogue** (name, text, selectable options; reads only while open) | stable on tested frames | dialogue translation, quest guides, text-to-speech |
| **Damage numbers** | beta (18 of 20 held-out numbers right) | damage meters, DPS logging |
| **Quest helper** text | beta | quest progress overlays |
| **Chat log** | beta | chat logging, translation |
| **Whole-screen text scan** (every line with its position) | works, ~250 ms, opt-in | anything without a dedicated reader |

Also: runs without touching the game process, a local-only server (loopback,
Origin-checked), a live dashboard page, Python and TypeScript examples, a
`MapleOcr::auto()` Rust API, and automatic calibration for your window size.

## How the numbers were measured

Reproduce: `pip install -r bench/requirements.txt`, then
`python bench/compare.py` (results in [bench/results.json](../bench/results.json)).

Caveats, stated plainly:

- One machine, one play session, 1920x1200 windowed. Small samples: 12 frames
  for HP/MP, 3 frames for tooltips. Treat the speed ratios as solid and the
  accuracy percentages as indicative.
- mpl-ocr's HP/MP/EXP digit sprites are **taught from your own screen** first
  (`mapleocr atlas learn`). 4 of the 12 frames above were used for teaching;
  on 16 frames never used for teaching, status bar fields were 100% correct,
  and across 150 frames of live play all fields read with no unknown glyph (8
  random frames checked by eye: 24 of 24 values right).
- The times are recognition time per read once the pixels are in memory.
  Screen capture itself costs about 0.5 ms for the needed regions, and is
  shared by all readers.
- The Python engines were not tuned beyond the usual advice (crop, upscale,
  invert and threshold for Tesseract). A model fine-tuned on this game's fonts
  would close the accuracy gap, but not the speed gap.
- Windows only for now (Windows Graphics Capture + the system OCR engine for
  chat and tooltip text).

# mpl-ocr design

Living document. Numbers are measured, not assumed; each one names its setup.

## Goals and constraints

- Read MapleStory Classic World game state from **screen pixels only**: no
  memory reading, injection, hooking, or packet inspection.
- Priority order: latency, then accuracy, then resource use.
- Windows first. Core in Rust; training tooling in Python.
- No game assets in the repo. Atlases, icon DBs, data packs, and fixtures are
  generated locally from the user's own captures (`fixtures/local/`,
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mapleocr\`).

## Crates

| crate | status | role |
|---|---|---|
| `mapleocr-capture` | M0 | target discovery/selection, WGC + DXGI backends, GPU ROI crop |
| `mapleocr-cli` | M0 | `targets`, `select`, `capture-dataset`, `bench capture` |
| `mapleocr-imgproc` | M1 | image views, resampling, NCC template search, xxh3 ROI hashing |
| `mapleocr-layout` | M1 | YAML ROI registry (anchor-relative), auto-calibration |
| `mapleocr-recog` | M1–M2 | `Recognizer` trait, `Reading`, preprocessing, glyph matcher, Windows OCR; icon and CRNN later |
| `mapleocr-semantic` | M1 (maps) | parsing + fuzzy snapping against user-built data packs |
| `mapleocr-core` | M1 | `MapleOcr` runtime: capture thread, dirty detection, cache, recognition worker |
| `mapleocr-py`, `mapleocr-server` | M5 | PyO3 bindings, WebSocket + shared memory + C ABI |

Crates get added in the milestone that needs them. There are no empty stubs.

## Capture

### Target selection
The user picks the target while the game runs; nothing depends on the install
path.

- `mapleocr targets` lists Alt+Tab-visible windows (HWND, PID, exe, client
  size, DPI) and monitors.
- `mapleocr select --index N` (or `--title`, `--process`, `--pid`, `--hwnd`,
  `--monitor`) saves a `TargetSelector` to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mapleocr\config.toml`.
  A window is saved as *process name + title*, not HWND, so a restarted client
  is picked up again.
- With nothing saved, a heuristic picks the largest window whose title or exe
  contains "maple".

### Backends
- **WGC** (`WgcBackend`): free-threaded frame pool; the `FrameArrived` callback
  signals an auto-reset Win32 event, and the consumer blocks on it, so there's no
  polling. Cursor capture is off (the cursor over an ROI would defeat dirty
  detection), and the capture border is turned off where the OS allows it. On wake, the
  backend drains to the newest frame. A content-size change recreates the pool and
  re-queries the client offset.
- **DXGI Desktop Duplication** (`DxgiBackend`): for exclusive fullscreen.
  Duplicates the game's monitor on the adapter that owns it and crops to the
  window's client rect. Mouse-only updates (`LastPresentTime == 0`) are skipped.
  `ACCESS_LOST` re-duplicates.
- **`Capture`** (the wrapper used by everything above): `Auto` opens WGC, and if no
  first frame arrives within 1.5 s and the window covers its monitor, it
  reopens on DXGI. If the target closes (`GraphicsCaptureItem.Closed` /
  `IsWindow`), it re-resolves the selector and rebinds with the same ROIs.
  Minimized windows simply produce no frames.
- The process is per-monitor-DPI-aware v2, so every coordinate is physical
  pixels (the dev machine runs at 120 DPI).

### GPU ROI crop
`RoiStager` owns one ROI-sized `STAGING` texture and one pre-allocated CPU
buffer per ROI. Per frame it queues all `CopySubresourceRegion`s, then maps
each, copies rows into the tight BGRA buffer, and unmaps. Parts of an ROI that
fall outside the frame are zeroed. Allocation-free unless the source format
changes.

### Timestamps
All timestamps are `Ticks` (100 ns) on the QPC timeline, the same clock as
WGC's `SystemRelativeTime`. Note: measured `present → acquired` is often
*negative* with WGC. `SystemRelativeTime` is the compositor's target vblank,
which lies slightly in the future when the frame is handed to us. Treat
`acquired → ready` as our capture cost. For true end-to-end latency, M1+ measures
`acquired → reading published`.

### M0 measurements
Setup: Ryzen 5 3600, RTX 3060 Ti, Windows 11, MapleStory client 1920×1200
windowed, release build.

| measurement | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| criterion, synthetic 1080p texture, 1 ROI 200×24 | 43 µs | | |
| criterion, 8 ROIs 200×24 | 104 µs | | |
| criterion, 32 ROIs 200×24 | 233 µs | | |
| criterion, full 1920×1080 frame | 1.81 ms | | |
| live WGC, 8 ROIs, `acquired → ready` | 0.46 ms | 1.96 ms | 2.78 ms |
| live WGC, full frame, `acquired → ready` | 2.20 ms | 2.84 ms | 3.74 ms |

Live, at about 57 fps delivered: **8 ROIs cost 6.2% of one core**, against 12.5% for
full-frame copies. The live p95 is dominated by `Map` waiting on a GPU that is
busy rendering the game. Candidate optimizations, to be measured before
they're adopted: double-buffered staging (map frame N-1 while N copies, which trades
one frame of latency, so probably not), a single atlas staging texture (one `Map`
instead of N), `MinUpdateInterval` to cap delivery rate per subscription.

## M1: map name end to end

```
capture thread                          recognition worker
  WGC frame ──► per-ROI xxh3 ──changed+settled──► raw-hash cache ─► preprocess (key, panel crop)
                 (unchanged: no work)              │                 └─► prepared-hash cache ─► WinOCR
                                                   └──────────────────────────────► parse + pack snap
                                                                  latest (ArcSwap, lock-free read) + subscribers (on change)
```

- **Layout** (`crates/mapleocr-layout/src/default_layout.yaml`): one anchor,
  the minimap's "MINI MAP" caption, and the `map_name` ROI relative to it, in
  native units (canvas 768 lines). The user can override it with
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mapleocr\layout.yaml`.
- **Calibration**: scale = client height / 768. On first run the anchor
  template is cut from the user's screen at its default position (only if
  it is textured, i.e. real UI) and saved to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mapleocr\anchors`.
  Later runs locate it by coarse-to-fine NCC; below 0.75 the default position is
  used. The runtime recalibrates when the client size changes.
- **Dirty detection**: xxh3 per ROI per frame. A ROI is sent for recognition
  only when its hash changed and then stayed stable for `settle_frames` (2 for
  the map name, which fades during map changes).
- **Two caches**: one on the raw ROI hash, and one on the hash of the
  *prepared* image (color-keyed + cropped to the minimap panel). The minimap
  width varies, so the ROI also covers animated world pixels; those change the
  raw hash but not the prepared one, so they never reach OCR.
- **Fallback OCR = `Windows.Media.Ocr`**, built into Windows, instead of
  PaddleOCR/ONNX for M1: no model download, no extra runtime, and it measured
  100% on our fixtures at ~3 ms. It sits behind `Recognizer`, so the ONNX engine
  can replace or complement it when the CRNN tier lands (M4).
- **Preprocessing** (measured): white-text key, panel crop, no upscale, 16 px
  padding. With 8 px padding Windows OCR dropped short second lines ("Henesys"),
  and 2× upscale was slower with no gain.
- **Semantic**: two lines → `{region, name}`; snapped to
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mapleocr\packs\maps.json` (built with `mapleocr pack
  add-map`) at similarity ≥ 0.75. Snapped readings carry confidence = similarity;
  unchecked ones carry 0.5.
- **Notifications** fire only when the value changes; `read()` always returns the
  latest (lock-free `ArcSwap`).
- The capture thread makes itself per-monitor DPI aware, so embedding apps don't
  have to. The example caught this: without it, a 125%-scaled desktop gave
  wrong ROIs.

Setup as in M0 (Ryzen 5 3600, 1920×1200 windowed, release build).

| measurement | result |
|---|---|
| `bench fixtures`: 20 labeled frames, 4 distinct maps | **100% exact** (region + name), with or without pack |
| OCR recognize time (WinOCR, incl. preprocessing) | p50 2.9 ms, p95 3.4 ms; first call ~14 ms (engine warm-up) |

Not yet: item tooltips (follow the cursor), inventory/equipment/stat/skill

### Glyph tier
Fixed-font UI text is read on the **native grid**:

1. Color-key the ROI (`luma`, `dark`, `white`, `#rrggbb`, `raw`).
2. Area-resample it back by the UI scale (×1.5625 at 1200 px). The sub-pixel
   grid phase is found once per ROI by maximizing variance over 16 quarter-pixel
   phases, then cached until the geometry changes. Without it, 1-px strokes fall
   between native pixels and 5/9 and 6/8 become indistinguishable.
3. Binarize halfway between background and ink. 0.4 merged neighbouring
   digits; 0.5 keeps them apart and keeps 1-px dots.
4. Split into lines (empty rows) and glyphs (empty columns), after erasing
   dashed underlines. A dashed underline is a 1-px-tall row of equal runs at an
   equal pitch; monospaced digits also have regular runs, but they're stacked,
   so they're kept.
5. Match each glyph by IoU with ±1 px tolerance. Two-segment merges handle the
   game's notched bold `n`/`m`/`h`. A DP split handles touching letters, using
   pair glyphs (`ft`, `tt`, …) rendered by GDI.

**Atlases** are built locally:
- `gdi:<face>:<px>[:bold]`: rendered 1-bit through GDI from the user's
  system font, plus every letter pair GDI draws touching. Accept IoU ≥ 0.70.
- `learned:<name>`: sprite glyphs cut from the user's own captures with
  `mapleocr atlas learn` (`--image` or live). Accept IoU ≥ 0.85, so an unlearned
  `8` can't pass as a `5`. Each character may hold variants (sub-pixel phase
  differs by position). Learning refuses lines whose labels look shifted (a
  segment already matches a different character at ≥ 0.95) and size-inconsistent
  variants.
- A number containing an unknown glyph is reported as text with confidence
  0.2, **never as a guessed number**.

### Optional windows (presence anchors)
An anchor with `optional: true` (the NPC dialogue's left border) is checked
before its window is read. The capture thread copies only the anchor strip,
a few hundred pixels: it tests the exact expected position first, falls back to
a ±3 px search, and re-checks a closed window every 4th frame. While the window is
closed its ROIs report `Hidden`, and their pixels never leave the GPU. Their
templates are learned from a saved frame with `mapleocr calibrate --learn-anchor`.

### Content-aware crops
- `panel`: stop where the panel color ends (minimap width varies).
- `band:#rrggbb`: keep the tallest band of rows dominated by a color (the NPC
  name plate's height depends on the portrait).

### CPU: what it cost and what fixed it
Measured with `mapleocr watch` (which prints a per-thread breakdown) at
~54–56 fps, all default ROIs:

| change | CPU, % of one core |
|---|---|
| first live run, all ROIs | 73 |
| glyph cache on binarized-bitmap hash; rate limits (chat 300 ms, quest 500 ms) | 35–39 |
| presence on the capture thread; strict learned threshold | 29–33 |
| copy only what is needed: closed windows and not-yet-due ROIs stay on the GPU | 27–32 |
| phase cached per ROI (quest helper 24–47 → 3–5 ms) | 19–21 |
| `screen` really opt-in (it was copying + hashing the full frame every frame) | 8.7–10.4 |
| `Map` polls without waiting, yields ≤ 1 ms, then sleeps (staging p50 0.48 ms) | **11.6–12.5** |

Blocking `Map` made the NVIDIA driver busy-wait while the GPU rendered the
game. Pure sleeping cut CPU most but raised staging latency to 2.5 ms p50.
Latency comes first, so the yield window stays. Remaining cost is mostly chat
OCR (~14 ms per read, ≤ 3.3 Hz). The 10%-of-a-core target is slightly exceeded
with every ROI on.

After the detectors were added (a full-frame scout every 250 ms): everything on
is ~19% of one core (detectors 5%, chat OCR ~4%, capture ~6%, quest helper
~1%); status bar + map only is ~6%. The 10% target holds for the HUD readers,
not for everything at once.

### Detectors: UI without a fixed position
A low-rate "scout" (every 250 ms) copies the full client frame and runs the
detectors on it; fixed ROIs never wait for it.

- **Tooltips** (item and skill; both use the same frame): found by the **title
  bullet**, a 7x7 px opaque sprite of one exact color (R~85, G~208, B~255) that
  sits at a fixed offset from the box corner. Unlike the translucent navy fill
  (which any dark blue sky also matches), it does not depend on what is behind
  the tooltip: 6 of 6 tooltips found at the exact pixel, none in frames without one.
  The first attempt (navy color + dilation + OCR) found names 4 of 5 times and was
  replaced.
  Reading: the box width comes from the next tooltip's corner, or from the white
  separator under the header (it ends 13 px before the right edge; item
  tooltips are all 369 px wide, skill tooltips grow to ~666 px). The icon frame is
  erased, then the region is resampled onto the native grid and read with the
  glyph matcher (Arial 12 regular/bold + 14 bold, built locally with GDI).
  Because the box is translucent, the right binarization depends on what is
  behind it, so each tooltip is read under 6 ink extractions and, per text
  line, the reading the font fits best wins (quality = sum of glyph
  similarities minus one point per unknown glyph). A reading is cached while
  the text pixels do not change. Cost: 20-30 ms to prepare, 10-60 ms to read.
  Matching uses popcounts on packed glyph rows, which also made every glyph
  reader about 2x faster.
  **Measured, against hand-labeled lines on the 6 distinct tooltips I have:
  names exact 5 of 6, text lines exact 15 of 25 (60%).** This is not good
  enough and is the main open item. Known failure classes: (1) red and gray
  text (the "-1" in "Weapon Def.: +5 (6 -1)", the REQ block) is invisible to
  the white-text key; (2) other UI showing through a tooltip that sits over a
  bright panel (the second tooltip in frame 5 over the quest helper: 0 of 4);
  (3) a few glyph confusions ("At" in "Attacks", a stray "l" after "Hat",
  "Remaining" with one unknown glyph); (4) the cursor covering text.
  The sample is far too small to claim any rate; a hover session across item
  types is needed (see "Tooltip plan" below).
- **Windows** (`kind: window`): a learned title template. The 1/4-frame search
  returns the 6 best candidates (a thin title strip alone matches the wrong
  place), each verified at full resolution. Re-checked at its last position
  every scout. Found on 4 of 4 frames with the inventory open, hidden on the
  rest. Slots are a grid relative to the title; each non-empty slot gets a
  4x4x RGB color descriptor (48 hex digits) matched by L1 distance against your
  local icon database (`mapleocr window name-icon`). 22 of 22 icons in one
  inventory had distinct descriptors; a gradient hash gave 4 identical ones.
- **Damage numbers** (beta): orange-mask blobs that are damage-sized (35-48 px
  tall at x1.56) and ringed by a white then a black outline (scenery such as
  mushroom caps and snail shells lacks the ring). Each digit is its own connected
  blob, because the outline separates neighbours, so blobs are classified one by
  one against a scale-normalized atlas (every digit resized to 24 px high; the
  sprites animate in size). Reading the number as a bitmap and cutting it by
  columns failed because digits overlap horizontally: 4 of 20 held-out numbers.
  Per-blob classification: **18 of 20 held-out numbers exactly right** (the
  atlas was taught from 15 other numbers of the same session), 1 wrong
  (101 read as 10), 1 missed. In 40 frames without large damage numbers there
  were 30 hits, all of them real digits; none came from scenery. Known issue:
  digits that bounce apart can be reported as separate one-digit hits instead of
  one number. Taught with `mapleocr atlas learn-damage`.

Known gaps: mesos (OCR reads only the first digit group), item quantities in
slots (need a taught `slot_digits` atlas), quest helper bold titles over dark
scenery, equipment/stat/skill windows (same `window` detector, not yet configured).

## Font identification (M0)

Tool: `tools/mapleocr_tools/identify_font.py` (Python, offline; see "Tooling"
below). Input is labeled text crops from `capture-dataset` frames. Method: render
each candidate word with **GDI, non-antialiased** (how a classic Win32 client
draws text), upscale by a candidate factor, take the best normalized
cross-correlation (NCC) against the capture, and score per word so small
advance-width differences don't accumulate across a line. GDI matters: Pillow/FreeType
hint 11–14 px differently, and with FreeType the best line score was only 0.70.

Data: 20 frames, windowed 1920×1200 at 120 DPI, one session, 8 labeled text
samples plus 2 status-bar samples.

### Findings

1. **UI scale is uniform ×1.5625 = client height / 768**, estimated at ×1.560.
   The client draws its UI on a 768-line canvas and the window stretches it with
   a **smooth filter** (bicubic/bilinear; nearest-neighbour scores clearly
   worse: 0.89 vs 0.96). The dark undershoot halos around strokes confirm a
   bicubic-type kernel. *An earlier note here claimed nearest-neighbour
   upscaling. That was wrong.*
   At ×25/16 the sub-pixel phase pattern repeats every 16 native = 25 screen
   pixels.
2. **The source text is 1-bit (non-antialiased) GDI Arial.** For every
   identified ROI, the non-AA render beats grayscale-AA and ClearType renders.

| ROI | font (native px) | NCC | margin to next family | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| item tooltip body | Arial 12 regular | 0.961 | 0.146 | identified |
| NPC dialogue + options | Arial 12 regular | 0.905 | 0.221 | identified |
| chat (incl. yellow system lines) | Arial 14 regular | 0.875 | 0.207 | probable |
| quest helper lines | Arial 11 regular | 0.867 | 0.090 | probable |
| quest helper titles | Arial 11 bold | 0.871 | 0.029 | probable |
| minimap map name | none (best Tahoma 11 bold) | 0.653 | 0.003 | unresolved |
| HP/MP/EXP numbers | none | 0.448 | n/a | unresolved: sprites |

"Probable" rows score lower because their crops sit on gradients or
translucent backgrounds; the font ranking itself is stable.

3. Text over translucent or busy backgrounds (chat log, `[Notice]` lines)
   **must be color-keyed** before matching. The yellow notice line scores 0.92
   keyed vs 0.37 on plain luma.
4. The map name is white with a drop shadow and doesn't match any installed
   font. It may be a stylized render or a font that isn't installed (Gulim/Dotum
   are absent on the dev machine). The client process is protected, so its
   install path can't be read from the process; `--client-dir` lets a user
   point the tool at their own install to try any font files there.

### Decisions

| ROI | engine | why |
|---|---|---|
| tooltip, NPC dialogue, quest helper, chat | **glyph matcher** | 1-bit Arial at known sizes. Templates are generated **locally on the user's machine** from the system's Arial via GDI, then upscaled with the measured kernel per sub-pixel phase (16 phases at ×25/16). Nothing is shipped. CRNN stays as the fallback for low confidence. |
| chat | glyph matcher **+ per-channel color key** (chat type colors) | translucent background |
| map name | **glyph atlas built from captures** (`build-atlas`) + data-pack snapping | font unresolved, but the set of map names is finite |
| HP/MP/EXP numbers | **sprite-digit matcher**, atlas from captures | sprite digits, ~12 symbols |
| damage numbers | sprite-digit matcher | visibly sprite-rendered (frames 15, 18–20) |
| inventory / item slots | icon matcher | grids of icons |

Open: confirm the scale model (`client height / 768`) at a second window size and
in fullscreen. The current data is all 1920×1200 windowed.

## Tooling

Offline analysis and training tools are Python, in `tools/` (`pip install -e
tools[dev]`; ruff + pyright + pytest). `identify-font` lives there instead of in
`mapleocr-cli` because it needs GDI rendering and array maths, never runs on
the hot path, and feeds the Python training pipeline.

```
python -m mapleocr_tools.identify_font fixtures/local/font-samples.json --out report.json
```
Samples and reports stay in `fixtures/local/` (git-ignored) because they contain
game pixels and text.
